questions.question: Why is `readFileSync` at module level generally acceptable, but inside a request handler it's not?
choices: Module-level sync operations run once at startup; request handlers run for every user request
readFileSync is only slow on Linux
It doesn't matter — both are equally bad
questions.explanation: Module-level readFileSync runs once when the server starts — a one-time delay is acceptable. Inside a request handler, it blocks the event loop for every single user request, causing the server to be unresponsive under load.

questions.question: What is the N+1 query problem?
choices: Querying the database one too many times
Running 1 query to fetch a list, then N separate queries for each item in the list
Having more than one database table
questions.explanation: N+1 queries happen when you fetch a list of items (1 query) then make a separate database call for each item (N queries). A single JOIN or batch query is much more efficient.

questions.question: Why is `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))` considered a performance anti-pattern?
choices: It's slower than a simple assignment
It serializes the entire object to a string then parses it back — wasteful for large payloads
It doesn't work with nested objects
It's been deprecated in modern JavaScript
questions.explanation: JSON.parse(JSON.stringify()) creates an intermediate string representation of the entire object. For large or deeply nested objects, this is significantly slower and more memory-intensive than using structuredClone() or a targeted copy.
